blocks.text: Bill Gates was born in Seattle on ==28 October 1955==. His full name was William H. Gates III, and the family called him "Trey", a card player's word for a three. He was the second of three children and the only son.

The Gates family was not new to Seattle. Bill's great-grandfather, also called William Henry Gates, moved there in the 1880s. On his mother's side, great-grandparents came from Nebraska to South Bend, Washington, in 1892. Trey was born into a family that had put down deep roots in the Pacific Northwest.

His parents met as students at the University of Washington. His father, William H. Gates Sr., was studying law. His mother, Mary Maxwell, earned an education degree in 1950. In the early 1950s they lived in Bremerton, where he worked as an assistant city attorney and she taught school.
Two parents who worked hard at their jobs and for their city.
The banker's daughter

Mary Maxwell was a banker's daughter from a wealthy banking family. At Roosevelt High School she was valedictorian and a star forward on the girls' basketball team. She was socially brilliant, the kind of person who put strangers at ease.

As her children grew, Mary built a huge civic career. She became the first woman to lead King County's United Way and the first woman to chair the national United Way's executive committee. She was the first woman director of First Interstate Bank of Washington, and in 1975 the governor appointed her to the University of Washington's Board of Regents, where she served for more than 18 years.

Bill's father became a successful Seattle lawyer and later a partner in a law firm. Berger describes him as tall, civil and quietly respected. Years later he still lived in the Lake Washington house where Trey grew up.

items.label: William H. Gates III born in Seattle
Mary Gates's service as a UW regent

blocks.text: The family lived in north Seattle, in the View Ridge and Laurelhurst neighbourhoods, which were mostly white and well-off. Gates does not pretend otherwise. In his 2025 memoir, Source Code, he wrote openly about luck: being born white, male and American in a society that favoured exactly those things.
It's impossible to overstate the unearned privilege I enjoyed
blocks.who: Bill Gates, Source Code (2025), quoted by Cascade PBS

blocks.text: So this is not a rags-to-riches story. The Seattle journalist Knute Berger put it bluntly: Gates grew up with every advantage and was no bootstrap success. __Knowing your head start is not weakness; it is the first step to using it well.__
Gami and the card table

A big figure in Trey's early life was his grandmother, Mary's mother, whom he called "Gami". She fed him Ritz crackers with peanut butter. Even more important, she and Mary loved card games, and they taught him how to play to win.
Sunday nights in the Gates house meant a big family dinner. Afterwards came bridge, the word game Password and trivia contests. Nobody played just for fun.
Winning mattered.
blocks.who: Bill Gates Sr., on the family games, to TIME (1997)

blocks.text: Summers were even more organised. Every year the family rented cabins at a place called Cheerio on Hood Canal, about two hours from Seattle. There were nightly campfires, family skits, a Saturday tennis tournament and a Sunday "Olympics". Trey liked solo sports best, such as water skiing.
He learned competition at the dinner table, long before business.

Mary ran the household with rules and rituals. Every Christmas the whole family got, and wore, matching pyjamas. When Trey was 7, she used her IBM Selectric typewriter to make a travel log for a family trip to Disneyland, for him and his older sister to fill in, with headings such as "land forms" and "population distribution".
At 8, Trey helped raise money for the Cub Scouts by selling ==179 pounds of nuts==. His memoir uses the number as an early sign of how hard he competed.
Rocking, and the fair of the future

His father remembered something odd from Trey's babyhood: he rocked back and forth in his cradle. He never really stopped. As an adult, Gates still rocked when he was thinking hard, and Microsoft staff picked up the habit.

In 1962, when Trey was six, Seattle hosted a World's Fair. The Gates family went to every pavilion. At the General Electric pavilion, Trey probably saw a vision of the future: electronic libraries and simulated home computers. Historians of his life see it as an early turning point.
It was a huge event, a neat deal. We went to every pavilion
blocks.who: Bill Gates, recalling the 1962 World's Fair (quoted by HistoryLink)

photo.caption: The Space Needle at Seattle's 1962 World's Fair. Six-year-old Trey's family went to every pavilion.
photo.author: Seattle Municipal Archives

blocks.text: At home he loved board games, especially Risk and Monopoly. He liked sports where he competed alone: roller skating, tennis, skiing. He was a keen Boy Scout and ended up only a few badges short of Eagle Scout.
"Have you ever tried thinking?"

Around age 9, something changed. Trey found he was very good at maths, and that gave him a belief that the world was rational and could be worked out by reasoning. It also made him, in his own words, a "bratty wiseass" who talked back to adults.
I became an adult overnight — an argumentative, intellectually forceful and sometimes not very nice adult.
blocks.who: Bill Gates, Source Code (2025), quoted in The New York Times; he adds he was about 9

blocks.text: By sixth grade he and his mother were in open conflict. He had a bedroom in the basement and often ignored her calls to dinner. One evening she called him over the house intercom and asked what he was doing.
"Yes, Mom, I'm thinking," he answered fiercely. Then came the line his family would never forget: "Have you ever tried thinking?" He was in sixth grade.
Every parent of a gifted, difficult kid will wince here.

His parents did something unusual for the 1960s. They took him to a psychologist in Seattle's University District, hoping to bring peace to the family and to understand their son. The counsellor gave Trey books by Freud to read between sessions, and the boy loved them.
He gave me books to read after each session, Freud stuff, and I really got into psychology theory.
blocks.who: Bill Gates, to TIME (1997)

blocks.text: After about a year of sessions and tests, the counsellor gave Mary his verdict: "You're going to lose." His advice, in effect, was to let Trey be himself. Bill Sr. said his strong-willed wife eventually accepted that competing with her son was pointless.
You had better just adjust to it because there's no use trying to beat him.
blocks.who: The family's counsellor, to Mary Gates, as reported by TIME (1997)

blocks.text: Read this twice. His parents chose to understand him, not crush him.

Today Gates describes himself as neurodivergent. When The Wall Street Journal printed an excerpt from his memoir, its headline asked if he was on the autism spectrum, and answered: "Probably." In the 1960s, almost nobody raised children with that idea in mind, which helps explain the clashes at home.

The next big decision was school. His father later said Trey was small and shy and needed protecting, and his parents thought a smaller class would suit a boy they saw as immature. Mary told Berger they did not want him bullied in a public school locker room, so they chose Lakeside, an elite private school across town.

items.text: William H. Gates III, "Trey", is born in Seattle.
Visits every pavilion at the Seattle World's Fair, aged six.
Mother types him a Disneyland travel log with headings like "land forms".
Sells 179 pounds of nuts for the Cub Scouts.
Becomes an "adult overnight": argumentative and sure the world is rational.
"Have you ever tried thinking?" Parents take him to a psychologist.
Parents move him to Lakeside, a private school across town.

blocks.title: Turn your fights into fuel
blocks.text: Trey's arguing could have wrecked his family. Instead, a counsellor and two patient parents pointed it at books, puzzles and goals. If you are the stubborn one, find adults who will aim your energy instead of fighting it. If you lead people, do the same for your stubborn ones.

Lakeside sat on a 33-acre, New England-style campus in north Seattle. In 1968 it did something almost no school in the world had done. Its Mothers' Club used money from a rummage sale to buy a teletype terminal for the students.

The terminal lived in one small room, next to an electric typewriter. It was linked by phone line to a General Electric GE-635 mainframe somewhere else in the city. Students typed commands, and a big remote computer typed back.

photo.caption: A Teletype ASR-33 at the Computer History Museum: a common terminal of the era for talking to faraway mainframes over a phone line.
photo.author: ArnoldReinhold

blocks.text: Computer time cost real money, and the Mothers' Club budget ran out fast. Parents helped pay the bills. Trey was about 13, and he was hooked.

A teacher named Bill Dougall ran the lab. He said Gates took just a week to learn more than he knew. Dougall also remembered the boy's favourite phrase, used on ideas he disliked: "That's the stupidest thing I've ever heard of!"
One week to overtake his teacher. Then he never stopped.
The older boy in the lab

In the autumn of 1968, Trey met a student nearly three years older named Paul Allen. Allen's father was associate director of the University of Washington libraries and his mother was a fourth-grade teacher. Trey quickly joined Allen's circle in the computer room.

photo.caption: Paul Allen (left) and Bill Gates at Lakeside School in 1970. Gates was about 14 here.
photo.author: Bruce Burgess

blocks.text: The two learned the BASIC programming language from a manual. In eighth grade Gates wrote a program that converted numbers between bases, then a tic-tac-toe game. He also built a computer version of Risk, inspired by Napoleon's battle plans.
Left to ourselves, Bill and I would program until we were starving
blocks.who: Paul Allen, in his memoir Idea Man (quoted by HistoryLink)

blocks.text: Out the basement door

School computer time was too short and too expensive. So the boys made a deal with a local company: they could use its computer for free if they hunted for bugs that made the machine crash. They were being paid, in effect, to break things.

Trey took this job seriously, maybe too seriously. His father later learned that he would slip out of the basement door after bedtime and spend most of the night at the computer. At home he was the difficult son; at the terminal he was a professional.
A neighbour of the Allens remembered seeing the lights on in Paul's room at 3 a.m. Allen, he said, "would be up there with that Gates kid, working on computer stuff."
Not everyone at Lakeside loved Trey. One classmate called him "an extremely annoying person", and some students enjoyed giving him a hard time. He was small, fast-talking and very sure he was right.

In ninth grade he invented his own kind of rebellion. He decided to get straight A's without ever taking a book home. He skipped maths class because he had already read ahead, and he still placed in the top ten nationally on a maths aptitude exam.
I came up with a new form of rebellion.
blocks.who: Bill Gates, to TIME (1997)

blocks.text: Rebellion, Gates-style: win so hard nobody can argue.
Kent

His best friend in these years was Kent Evans, the son of a Unitarian minister. The two boys read Fortune magazine together, the way other kids read comics. Decades later, Gates said he could still remember Kent's phone number.
We read Fortune together; we were going to conquer the world.
blocks.who: Bill Gates, on Kent Evans, to TIME (1997)

blocks.text: Gates, Allen, Kent and another friend, Ric, spent all their free time writing more and more ambitious programs. On hiking trips Gates was a follower. In the computer room, he wrote later, he was the leader.
Unlike in hiking, among that group of friends, I was the leader.
blocks.who: Bill Gates, Source Code (2025), WSJ excerpt

blocks.text: The pencil résumé

The boys called themselves the Lakeside Programmers Group, and they wanted real work. In ==November 1970==, a time-sharing company in Portland, Oregon, offered them a contract to write a payroll program. The payment was free time on its mainframe.
Gates had just turned 16. His résumé for the payroll job was written in pencil on lined notebook paper. As Allen later wrote: "We got the job."
The project nearly split the friends. Allen tried to take the work over, then found he needed Gates's coding help. Gates agreed to come back, but only on one condition.
O.K., but I'm in charge, and I'll get used to being in charge, and it'll be hard to deal with me from now on unless I'm in charge.
blocks.who: Bill Gates, recalling what he told Paul Allen, to TIME (1997)

blocks.text: Sixteen, and already fighting for control. Watch this pattern.
That sentence is a preview of the next 30 years. __Gates learned early that whoever writes the hardest code can set the terms.__ It made him powerful, and it also made him hard to work with.
Fifty miles in the snow

Computers were not his only world. From about 13, Gates joined a breakaway group of five Boy Scouts who took long, unsupervised hikes. Over roughly three years they covered hundreds of miles in the Olympic Mountains, the Glacier Peak Wilderness and along the Pacific coast, living on Spam, Hamburger Helper and instant breakfast.
We wanted more freedom and more risk than the trips the Scouts offered.
blocks.who: Bill Gates, Source Code (2025), WSJ excerpt

blocks.text: He was not the star of these trips. He was the skinniest and usually the coldest, and he felt weaker than the others. But he loved being far from help, making real decisions about food, routes and risk.

In ==June 1971==, at the end of his sophomore year, the group tried a roughly 50-mile route through the Olympic Mountains, over the Low Divide and down to the Quinault River. Heavy snow made the going brutal. When they reached a snowed-in shelter, the leader called a vote on whether to go on, and Gates was on the losing side.

So he kept walking, and he kept coding in his head. He was writing a version of BASIC for a small PDP-8 computer that a teacher friend could use, and it had only six kilobytes of memory, so every instruction had to count. Step by step through the snow, he worked out the part of the program that evaluates formulas.
I'd picture the code and then try to trace how the computer would follow my commands.
blocks.who: Bill Gates, Source Code (2025), WSJ excerpt

blocks.text: Stuck on a problem? Walk. He debugged code on a mountain.
Pages, girls and traffic

Gates's parents knew powerful people, and doors opened. In spring 1971 a family friend, Washington governor Daniel Evans, arranged for him to serve as a page in the state legislature in Olympia. In summer 1972 Congressman Brock Adams arranged a paid job as a congressional page in Washington, D.C.

Back at Lakeside, the school hired him to write a program that scheduled classes, and paid him ==$4,200==. He built in a secret feature. He arranged his own timetable so that his history class had only one other boy and, as he put it, "all the good girls in the school".

He and his friends also started a business that analysed and graphed traffic data for local governments. One history of Microsoft says the traffic program earned Gates and Allen $20,000 in one summer. For two teenagers in the early 1970s, that was serious money.

items.label: Gates's age at the first paid contract (payroll, Nov 1970)
Paid by Lakeside for the class-scheduling program
Reported earnings from the traffic-data program in one summer
Memory he had to squeeze his PDP-8 BASIC into

blocks.text: His father watched him change. As a teenager Trey grew more confident and funnier, a good storyteller who could imitate people's voices, and he made peace with his mother. He even acted, playing a lead role in Peter Shaffer's comedy Black Comedy in the school chapel.
Some things stayed hard. Girls, in particular, were a different kind of problem from code. His father remembered this scene clearly.
I remember him fretting for two weeks before asking a girl to the prom, then getting turned down.
blocks.who: Bill Gates Sr., to TIME (1997)

blocks.text: The friend who did not come back
Then Kent Evans died in a mountain-climbing fall. Gates was asked to speak at the funeral, but he could not do it. For about two weeks afterwards, he could barely function at all.
I had never thought of people dying.
blocks.who: Bill Gates, on Kent Evans's death, to TIME (1997)

blocks.text: Grief pushed him closer to Paul Allen. The two learned an artificial-intelligence programming language together and took on odd programming jobs. They became the partnership that would build Microsoft.
We were true partners. We'd talk for hours every day.
blocks.who: Bill Gates, on Paul Allen, to TIME (1997)

blocks.text: Grief can redirect a life. It redirected his.
A real job at 17

In his senior year, the defence contractor TRW came calling. It was behind schedule on software for the Bonneville Power Administration, which ran the electric grid of the Pacific Northwest, and it wanted Gates's help debugging it. Gates phoned Allen, who was by then at Washington State University.

Both were offered jobs at ==$165 a week==. Gates took leave from Lakeside, Allen took leave from college, and the two rented an apartment together in Vancouver, Washington. Gates was 17 and working on software for a real power grid.

He went back to Seattle to finish high school, already accepted to Harvard. The plan, on paper, was a normal elite education. In reality he had already spent five years programming, much of it for pay.

Meets Paul Allen in the computer room.
Gets a payroll contract in Portland, paid in computer time. He has just turned 16.
Serves as a page in the Washington state legislature.
Codes BASIC in his head on a 50-mile snowy hike.
Paid $4,200 for Lakeside's scheduling program; congressional page in D.C.
Works for TRW on power-grid software for $165 a week.

blocks.title: Get paid to learn
blocks.text: Gates never waited for a degree to start working. He traded bug-hunting for computer time, pencilled a résumé at 16 and took a grown-up contract at 17. Find someone with a problem you can almost solve, and offer to solve it for whatever they can pay, even if that is only access.

Gates arrived at Harvard in the autumn of 1973, just short of his 18th birthday. Allen had warned him that Harvard would be harder than Lakeside and that some students would be better at maths. Gates's reply was two words: "No way."

Allen was right. Gates met people who were as good at maths as he was, or better, and that pushed him to look harder at other interests. Being the smartest person in the room had been his identity, and now it was not guaranteed.
Being humbled at 18 is cheap. Being humbled at 40 costs more.
He lived in Currier House, at the Radcliffe end of campus. His room became a late-night hangout, partly because everyone knew he did not care about getting up in the morning.
There were always lots of people in my dorm room late at night discussing things
blocks.who: Bill Gates, Harvard Commencement speech (2007)

blocks.text: His study method was unusual. He skipped lectures for courses he was enrolled in, sat in on lectures for courses he was not taking, and crammed before exams. He later admitted he had "this terrible habit of not ever attending classes".
I used to sit in on lots of classes I hadn't even signed up for. That's how I came to be the leader of the anti-social group.
blocks.who: Bill Gates, Harvard Commencement speech (2007)

blocks.text: Copy the curiosity, not the skipping.
Poker until six
In his sophomore year, a student named Steve Ballmer lived down the hall. Ballmer, who would one day succeed Gates as Microsoft's chief executive, watched his new friend's nights closely.
He'd play poker until 6 in the morning, then I'd run into him at breakfast and discuss applied mathematics.
blocks.who: Steve Ballmer, to TIME (1997)

blocks.text: Ballmer pulled Gates into a social life. He got him into an eating club, where Gates gave a drunken initiation speech about an artificial-intelligence machine. They played Pong in hamburger joints and went to Studio 54 on trips to New York. Ballmer called him "the smartest guy I've ever met".
The pancake problem

In a combinatorics class, professor Harry Lewis described a puzzle that was easy to state but unsolved. You have a messy stack of pancakes of different sizes, and the only move allowed is to slide a spatula under some of them and flip that top part over. What is the smallest number of flips that will always sort the stack?
this smart sophomore comes into my office and explains that he's got a five-thirds N algorithm
blocks.who: Harvard professor Harry Lewis, to NPR (2008), on Gates returning a day or two later

blocks.text: The simple method takes about two flips per pancake. Gates's method needed about five-thirds of a flip per pancake, roughly 1.67. With a young Harvard assistant professor, Christos Papadimitriou, he published it in the journal Discrete Mathematics in ==1979==.

It was real mathematics, not a party trick. Lewis called the approach "quite clever", and it needed a complicated case analysis. When researchers finally beat it, decades later, their strategy was only about 1 percent faster, and they needed powerful computers to find it.
Billionaire later; published mathematician first.
The Aiken lab

Harvard's computer centre was the Aiken Computer Laboratory. Professor Thomas Cheatham of the Aiken lab saw both sides of the young programmer. He called Gates "a hell of a good programmer", but said he also "put people down when it was not necessary".

Allen did not want to lose his partner to Boston. In 1974, at Gates's urging, Allen left Washington State to take a programming job at Honeywell in Massachusetts, driving his Chrysler across the country. Gates had also been offered a Honeywell job; he stayed in college but worked there in the summer of 1974.
The magazine cover

In December 1974, Allen was walking through Harvard Square when he saw the new issue of Popular Electronics. Its cover story was the Altair 8800, a computer kit built around Intel's 8080 chip. Allen bought it and ran to Gates's dorm.
I saw a cover of Popular Electronics with this thing that looked like what I had been imagining
blocks.who: Paul Allen, in PBS's Triumph of the Nerds (1996)

blocks.text: The Altair kit cost ==$397== and came with just 256 bytes of memory. You programmed it by flipping switches on the front panel. It had no language that normal people could use, and Gates saw the gap at once.
Paul showed that to me and then okay, here was a company that would be needing software.
blocks.who: Bill Gates, in PBS's Triumph of the Nerds (1996)

photo.caption: An original 1975 Altair 8800 with a Teletype terminal. Gates and Allen's BASIC made machines like this usable.
photo.author: Tim Colegrove

blocks.text: Selling what did not exist

In January 1975, Gates picked up the phone in Currier House and called the company in Albuquerque, New Mexico, that made the Altair, called MITS. He offered to sell them software for it. There was one problem.
Instead they said: "We're not quite ready, come see us in a month," which was a good thing, because we hadn't written the software yet.
blocks.who: Bill Gates, Harvard Commencement speech (2007)

blocks.text: He sold it before it existed. Then he built it, fast.

For the next eight weeks or so, Gates and Allen wrote a version of BASIC for the Altair, using Harvard's computers. A Harvard student named Monte Davidoff joined them to help. Their code had never run on a real Altair, so they were writing software for a machine they could only read about.
Gates was proud of that code all his life. In 1996 he told a documentary crew that it had been a labour of love.
that was er, er, a work of love, you know, we just kept tuning and tuning that thing.
blocks.who: Bill Gates, in PBS's Triumph of the Nerds (1996)

blocks.text: Then came the question of who would fly to Albuquerque to show it off. Allen went. In his telling, he looked like an adult, while Gates could pass for a high-school sophomore.
Allen flew with the program on paper tape and loaded it into an Altair at MITS. It had never run on a real machine before. He was terrified it would fail in front of the customer.
I was just I was so nervous....this is just....it's not going to work and it worked.
blocks.who: Paul Allen, on the first demo at MITS, in PBS's Triumph of the Nerds (1996)

items.label: Time to write Altair BASIC at Harvard
Paid by MITS on signing, plus royalties

blocks.text: MITS signed a contract. Gates and Allen got ==$3,000== on signing, plus a royalty on each copy shipped with the hardware. MITS also hired Allen as its director of software, and in April 1975 he moved to Albuquerque.
Sixty–forty
In the summer of 1975, Gates joined Allen in Albuquerque. They formed a partnership they first called "Micro-Soft". Allen had assumed they would split it 50-50.
Gates disagreed. Allen was drawing a salary from MITS, he argued, while Gates had written BASIC at Harvard for nothing. He insisted on 60-40 in his favour, and later the split moved to 64-36.
It's not right for you to get half
blocks.who: Bill Gates to Paul Allen, as recalled in Allen's Idea Man (quoted by HistoryLink)

blocks.text: Gates won that argument, but it had a cost. The two fought often in the years that followed, and the friendship that began over a teletype was later badly strained. __Winning a negotiation with your co-founder is not the same as winning.__
Very important for first-time founders! Talk about equity early and fairly.

Life in Albuquerque was scrappy. The young partners lived across the street from MITS at the Sundowner Motel, and a MITS colleague remembered days when Gates slept on the floor of the software lab. Gates never used his family inheritance to fund the company.

Harvard faded away. The fall term of 1975 was, by one account, his last real term, and he left against his parents' wishes; another account says he formally left in January 1977, technically on extended leave. Gates once summed up the start simply.
We started when I was 19.
blocks.who: Bill Gates, in PBS's Triumph of the Nerds (1996)

blocks.text: The bedroom-basement rebel had become a company founder. He had the tools: years of paid programming, a partner he trusted and a product that worked. What came next, from a motel in New Mexico to the biggest software company on Earth, is the story of the next chapters.

About eight weeks of coding; Allen's demo in Albuquerque works first time.
Allen moves to Albuquerque as MITS's director of software.
Gates joins him; "Micro-Soft" is born, split 60-40.

blocks.title: Sell the future, then deliver it
blocks.text: Gates called MITS before a single line of code existed, then worked day and night to make his promise true. That only works because he had spent seven years learning to code. Promise boldly only what your skills can realistically deliver, and then deliver it early.

factCheck.method: Every claim was traced to fetched, reliable sources: Walter Isaacson's 1997 TIME cover story (interviews with Gates, his father, Paul Allen and Steve Ballmer); HistoryLink.org's essays on Bill Gates, Mary Maxwell Gates, Paul Allen, Lakeside School and Microsoft (which cite the Manes/Andrews biography and Allen's memoir Idea Man); Gates's own 2025 memoir Source Code via the Wall Street Journal excerpt and reviews in The New York Times and Cascade PBS; Gates's 2007 Harvard commencement speech (Harvard Gazette); the PBS documentary Triumph of the Nerds (1996 transcript); The Harvard Crimson; NPR; the Crossref/DOI record of Gates's 1979 paper; and Fortune. Quotes were checked word for word against the fetched pages. Wikipedia was used only as a map of leads and is never cited. Photos come from Wikimedia Commons, with author and licence read from the Commons API.

disputed.claim: How old Gates and Allen were when they met
disputed.note: Fortune (2018) says Gates was 12 and Allen 14. HistoryLink says they met in fall 1968, when Allen was 15; Gates turned 13 that October. The text says 'about 13' and 'autumn of 1968'.

disputed.claim: When Gates wrote Lakeside's class-scheduling program
disputed.note: TIME (1997) places it in tenth grade. HistoryLink says 1972, when Gates was 17, and gives the $4,200 fee. The text gives no grade, only the fee, with 1972 in the timeline.
HistoryLink's Gates essay says fall 1975 was his last term. HistoryLink's Microsoft essay says he left in January 1977, technically on extended leave. Both are given in the text.

Gates has long said programming pulled him away. The Harvard Crimson (2004) notes that a 1993 biography says he left after Harvard objected to his use of university computers for private business, and quotes his father: 'There was a flap, no question about it.' The text does not state either cause as fact; for later chapters.

HistoryLink's Microsoft essay reports $20,000 in one summer; TIME calls the business 'profitable' without a figure. The text attributes the number. The business name 'Traf-O-Data' is widely reported but could not be confirmed in a fetched reliable source this session, so it is not used.

HistoryLink's Gates essay says summer 1975; HistoryLink's Microsoft essay says 'by fall 1975'. The commonly cited 4 April 1975 founding date was not confirmed in a fetched source, so the text says summer 1975.
